heading: React 19: useState()
summary: Hold a value across renders and request new renders when updating state. React reads the state snapshot from the current render; the setter queues future work.
parameters: initialValue: the value (or initializer function) for the first render.
returns: [currentValue, setValue] — current render snapshot and a stable setter.
commonMistakes: Expecting the count variable to update immediately after calling setCount.
Mutating arrays or objects held in state instead of creating fresh values.
securityPerformanceNotes: Use updater functions for queued changes based on previous state.
Avoid sensitive data in browser state; it is not an authorization boundary.

heading: React 19: useEffect()
summary: Synchronize an already-rendered component with a non-React system. Declare all reactive dependencies and return cleanup for listeners, timers and subscriptions.
parameters: setup: function invoked after commit; dependencies: reactive values used by setup.
returns: void; optional cleanup function executes before a rerun and on unmount.
commonMistakes: Using Effects to derive data already available from props or state.
Omitting cleanup or reactive dependencies, causing stale subscriptions.
securityPerformanceNotes: Effects do not run while rendering static server HTML.
Do not read secrets in browser Effects or bypass authenticated API boundaries.

heading: React 19: useReducer()
summary: Model related transitions as explicit actions processed by a pure reducer, keeping mutation and validation decisions separate from rendering.
parameters: reducer: pure function (state, action) => nextState; initialState: starting value.
returns: Current state and a stable dispatch function.
commonMistakes: Performing fetches or mutations inside the reducer.
Returning the same mutated state object instead of a new state.
securityPerformanceNotes: Keep reducers deterministic so they can be tested without a network.
Validate and authorize any eventual server mutation independently.

heading: React 19: useRef()
summary: Keep a mutable value stable between renders without scheduling a render when its current property changes. Common uses include timer handles and DOM focus.
parameters: initialValue: initial ref.current; frequently null for DOM elements.
returns: Stable object with mutable current property.
commonMistakes: Expecting ref.current changes to render new text on screen.
Dereferencing a DOM node before React has committed it.
securityPerformanceNotes: Never use refs to bypass authorization or hide client-visible secrets.
Clean up timers and subscriptions referenced by refs on unmount.

heading: React 19: useContext()
summary: Read the nearest matching provider value in the component tree. Use context for shared values, but avoid sending unrelated fast-changing state through broad providers.
parameters: MyContext: context object created with createContext.
returns: The nearest provider value, or the declared default when no provider exists.
commonMistakes: Assuming context state automatically persists across browser sessions.
Putting every rapidly changing field into one enormous provider.
securityPerformanceNotes: Context is a UI data channel, not an authentication or permission mechanism.
Minimize provider scope to reduce unnecessary consumer updates.

heading: React 19: useTransition()
summary: Mark non-urgent state transitions so urgent input remains responsive, while exposing an isPending flag for accessible progress feedback.
parameters: scope: callback scheduling updates that React may treat as non-blocking.
returns: isPending Boolean and startTransition scheduling function.
commonMistakes: Wrapping the controlled input's urgent value update in a transition.
Assuming a transition eliminates expensive synchronous calculations or network costs.
securityPerformanceNotes: Do not treat isPending as proof that a server mutation succeeded.
Measure user-perceived responsiveness rather than assuming transitions are always faster.

heading: React 19: useOptimistic()
summary: Render a temporary projected state while an Action is pending. Reconcile to the server-confirmed value when the operation completes or fails.
parameters: state: confirmed source; updateFn: pure projection of current state and pending input.
returns: Projected state and a function to enqueue an optimistic update within an Action.
commonMistakes: Treating a temporary optimistic item as confirmed persistence.
Failing to reconcile after errors, resulting in ghost or duplicate records.
securityPerformanceNotes: Enforce authorization and validation on the server regardless of optimistic UI.
Use stable client IDs and idempotent server operations where retries are possible.

heading: React 19: useActionState()
summary: Track the returned state and pending status of a form Action. A form Action receives previous state first, followed by submitted form input.
parameters: action: async reducer receiving prior state and form payload; initialState: default result.
returns: Latest Action result, formAction function, pending Boolean.
commonMistakes: Using the wrong parameter order when binding the Action.
Returning sensitive exception messages or assuming the client form enforces authorization.
securityPerformanceNotes: Validate unknown form fields and authorize inside the actual server mutation.
Use visible pending and error feedback; do not reveal private stack traces.

heading: Next.js 16: page.tsx
summary: Make a route publicly accessible with an App Router page file. Page components are Server Components by default; dynamic params are promised and must be awaited.
syntax: export default async function Page({params}: {params: Promise<{slug:string}>}) { ... }
parameters: params: Promise of dynamic route segments (for a dynamic route); optional searchParams also arrives asynchronously.
returns: A React UI tree for the URL path; the function may be async on the server.
commonMistakes: Treating dynamic params as synchronous in Next 16.
Assuming a route slug alone proves authorization to load a private record.
securityPerformanceNotes: Validate dynamic path values and check object-level permission on protected resources.
Server rendering does not guarantee a route avoids private-data caching risks.

heading: Next.js 16: route.ts GET/POST
summary: Implement a server-side HTTP endpoint using Web Request and Response APIs. Validate all inputs, choose an explicit caching policy and authorize before returning private data.
syntax: export async function GET(request: Request): Promise<Response> { ... }
parameters: request: standard Web Request; optional context with awaited dynamic params.
returns: Response with status, headers and a serialized body.
commonMistakes: Returning 200 for invalid JSON or failed authorization.
Building outbound fetch URLs from unvalidated caller-supplied hosts (SSRF).
securityPerformanceNotes: Validate both input shape and authenticated principal at the handler boundary.
Use private no-store responses for account-specific resources.

heading: Next.js 16: dynamic route segments
summary: Represent variable route portions with bracketed folders such as [slug] and [[...segments]]. Await promised params in Next.js 16 server routes.
parameters: slug: path segment value supplied by the URL; catch-all routes may return arrays of segments.
returns: A params object promised to the page, route handler or metadata generator.
commonMistakes: Confusing a route-group folder with a public URL segment.
Using path data directly as an authorized database selector without scoping.
securityPerformanceNotes: Validate slug format before performing database work.
Perform server-side authorization even when navigation to a URL is hidden in the UI.

heading: Next.js 16: Server Actions
summary: Execute server-side mutations from forms or Client Components. Server Actions are remotely invokable endpoints: validate inputs and permissions on every invocation.
syntax: async function action(formData: FormData) { 'use server'; /* validate */ }
parameters: formData: submitted form fields; bound inputs must still be validated and authorized.
returns: Promise resolving with a response/Action state; may trigger cache invalidation after successful persistence.
commonMistakes: Assuming the form button being hidden or disabled enforces authorization.
Invalidating caches before a committed database transaction.
securityPerformanceNotes: Validate and authorize again inside each Server Action, not just in the browser.
Apply idempotency and CSRF/origin defenses as appropriate.

heading: Next.js 16: use cache
summary: Opt in to caching a public deterministic function or component under the Cache Components model. Requires cacheComponents enabled in next.config; avoid placing user-bound private data into shared cache scopes.
syntax: async function cachedData(){ 'use cache'; cacheLife('hours'); return publicData; }
parameters: cacheLife: lifetime profile; cacheTag: optional domain invalidation label.
returns: Cached function result subject to the configured cache profile and invalidation rules.
minimalExample:
import {cacheLife} from 'next/cache';
export async function publicTopics(){'use cache';cacheLife('hours');return ['React','Next'];}
commonMistakes: Assuming use cache works without enabling the correct version-specific configuration.
Caching session cookies, private profile rows or credentials in a shared cache scope.
securityPerformanceNotes: Do not cache user-specific private results in a shared key.
Choose tags and lifetime profiles based on actual freshness requirements.

heading: Next.js 16: cacheTag()
summary: Label cached domain results so a successful mutation can invalidate related entries. cacheTag belongs inside an explicit cached scope.
parameters: tag: stable domain label, unique enough to avoid unrelated cache invalidation.
returns: void; associates the cached result with an invalidation tag.
minimalExample:
import {cacheTag} from 'next/cache';
export async function getCatalog(){'use cache';cacheTag('catalog:academy');return ['React'];}
commonMistakes: Using one global tag for all unrelated data, causing broad invalidation.
Putting unbounded private/session identifiers into globally shared tags.
securityPerformanceNotes: Do not use cache tags as an authorization mechanism.
Invalidate after a successful write and keep the tag namespace stable.

heading: Next.js 16: revalidateTag()
summary: Mark cached data with a tag for revalidation. In current Next.js APIs, the 'max' profile supports stale-while-revalidate semantics; updateTag is used for read-your-own-writes in Server Actions.
parameters: tag: domain label; profile: cache lifetime/revalidation behavior such as max.
returns: void; requests revalidation rather than returning fresh data synchronously.
commonMistakes: Using revalidateTag('tag') without the recommended current cache profile.
Expecting a stale-while-revalidate operation to guarantee immediate fresh reads.
securityPerformanceNotes: Never invalidate as a substitute for actual data persistence.
Scope cache tags by public domain rather than private user secrets.

heading: Next.js 16: proxy.ts
summary: A special root proxy.ts file performs lightweight request-time routing and response handling; Next.js 16 renamed Middleware to Proxy. Proxy does not replace authorization inside handlers and data services.
syntax: export function proxy(request: NextRequest) { return NextResponse.next(); }
parameters: request: NextRequest, with path and headers; config.matcher controls matched requests.
returns: NextResponse that passes through, rewrites or redirects an incoming request.
minimalExample:
import {NextResponse,type NextRequest} from 'next/server';
export function proxy(_request:NextRequest){return NextResponse.next();}
commonMistakes: Assuming a Proxy redirect is equivalent to per-resource authorization.
Using Proxy to call privileged database services without robust identity checks.
securityPerformanceNotes: Check ownership and RBAC/RLS inside protected services and route handlers.
Use Proxy for limited routing/header work; do not claim it secures an API by itself.
